To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) telomere length is a marker of high-dose exposure, but not of low-doses, (ii) m-FISH is a sensitive technique for the detection of chromosome damage after low-dose exposure and (iii) the use of primary human fibroblasts as in vitro model is an appropriate tool to study the biological effects of low doses of ionizing radiation.

1) the m-FISH technique is more sensitive than the q-FISH technique for the detection of chromosome aberrations induced by X-rays in primary fibroblastic cells; 2) the m-FISHe technique is suitable for the assessment of chromosome aberrations at low doses; 3) unstable aberrations, induced at 0.1 and 0.2 Gy, are the best marker of low doses of radiation.
the m-FISH technique, compared to q-FISH, is more sensitive to detect chromosome damage induced by low-dose radiation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new in vitro system to detect low-dose X-rays in terms of cytogenetic damage in human primary fibrobasts, by comparing two FISH techniques.
the setup of an efficient and reliable in vitro system to study low-dose X-rays as measured in cytogenetic damage, in human primary fiboblasts.

the setup of an efficient and reliable in vitro system to assess the cytogenetic damage in human primary cells induced by low-dose of ionizing radiation, in order to use it for retrospective dosimetric purposes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the m-FISH technique is a good choice for the study of low dose effects in human cells.
the use of q-FISH is unsuitable for the assessment of low exposures, while m-FISH is a good tool to assess the induction of both stable and unstable chromosome aberrations in human fibroblasts.
m-FISH is a more sensitive technique than q-FISH in the detection of low doses, and that it can be applied in the in vitro assessment of cytogenetic damage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

q-FISH is not suitable to report low doses while m-FISH, with its sensitivity to detect both unstable and stable aberrations, is the best technique to study cytogenetic damage in low-dose X-rays exposed human primary fibroblast.
the m-FISH technique is the most promising for low-dose cytogenetic studies in vitro, but further investigations are needed for a better understanding of the mechanism of action.
m-FISH is a good tool to assess the chromosome instability induced by low X-ray doses in human primary fibrosarcoma.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to be used as biomarkers, the chosen technique should be able to provide a good sensitivity and a good specificity.
, in the in vitro low-dose range, the m-FISH approach is the most suitable for the assessment of cytogenetic damage.
m-FISH is a reliable technique to report low exposures, and the best one to date for retrospective dosimetric applications.
